problemText: A geographer describes a library by saying 'The library is at 54 Main Street.' What kind of location is this?
choices: An absolute location, because a street address points to one exact building no matter who reads it
A relative location, because the street name tells you where it is in relation to another landmark or place that you already know
An absolute location, because it uses a direction word to help people find it using a compass
A relative location, because the description depends on someone knowing what Main Street is and where it connects to other places
hints: Does this description depend on knowing where another place is, or does it work by itself?
Would the same street address point to the same building whether you are reading it from across town or across the world?

problemText: A student wants to describe where the playground is. She says, 'The playground is three blocks north of the school.' Why can this description fail to work for some people?
choices: Because three blocks is not an exact measurement that all mapmakers agree on
Because someone who has never heard of the school will not know where to find the playground
Because the playground's real location is fixed and should not depend on the school
Because a relative location can only be used if the playground is actually north of something
hints: What is the name for the already-known place that a relative location uses to describe another place?
What happens to a relative location if the person listening does not know where the reference point is?

problemText: Two people describe the same restaurant in two ways: Person A says it is at '217 Oak Avenue.' Person B says it is 'next to the hardware store.' Which statement does not depend on the listener already knowing something else?
choices: Person B's statement, because 'next to' is a clear direction
Neither statement works without knowing something else first
Person A's statement, because a street address works the same way for everyone
Both statements work equally well because they both describe the restaurant's exact location
hints: Does Person A's description change if you have never heard of Oak Avenue before?
What must a person already know in order to understand Person B's description?

problemText: A shop has the street address '93 Pine Road.' Three different customers describe its location three different ways: 'across from the bank,' 'one block south of the park,' and 'in the same building as the dentist.' How many of these four descriptions are absolute locations?
choices: Four—they all describe the same shop, so they all point to one exact spot
Two—the street address and the description about the dentist's building
Three—all of them, because they are all precise
One—only the street address
hints: Remember: a description that names another place as a reference point is relative, not absolute, no matter how precise it is.
How many of the customer descriptions depend on knowing where the bank, the park, or the dentist is?

problemText: A student wrote: 'The park is an absolute location because I can describe exactly where it is—it's two miles east of downtown.' What error did the student make?
choices: The description uses downtown as a reference point, so it is a relative location, not absolute
Two miles is not precise enough to be absolute; true absolute locations require latitude and longitude coordinates or a specific street address instead
The student used a direction word and a distance measurement together, which means the location depends on knowing where downtown is as a starting reference point
An absolute location must always use a street address, and distances measured in miles can only be used when describing relative locations with a known reference point
hints: Does the description 'two miles east of downtown' depend on knowing where downtown is?
What is the name for the place that a relative location depends on?

problemText: A map shows both a museum and a train station. The museum's absolute location is '145 Central Boulevard.' The train station's absolute location is '89 Riverside Drive.' A tour guide tells visitors, 'The museum is just two blocks south of here'—pointing to where they are standing at the train station. Why does the tour guide's description of the museum's location make sense to the visitors, even though she never told them the museum's street address?
choices: Because a relative location describes a place by comparing it to a known reference point, and the visitors use that comparison to understand where to go instead of needing a street address
Because the visitors already know where they are standing, so the relative location gives them enough information to find the museum
Because a street address and a direction word describe the same type of location information, so 'south' is another way of stating what a street address would tell them
Because the tour guide's method of using nearby landmarks and distances to describe where something is located is identical to how an absolute location pinpoints a place on a map
hints: What is the reference point in the guide's description? Do the visitors already know where that place is?
The guide does not use a street address. What does she use instead, and why does it work?

problemText: Which of the following best describes what geography is the study of?
choices: Only the mountains, rivers, and oceans on Earth, leaving out all human settlements, cultures, and activities
The names and capitals of every country in the world, focusing on memorizing political divisions and borders
Earth's physical and human features and how they relate to each other
Only the cities and countries where people live, excluding natural landforms and climate patterns
hints: Geography is about more than just learning names — it asks questions about places.
Think about whether geography studies only nature or only people, or both together.

problemText: A student learns that a desert has very little rainfall and hot daytime temperatures. Is this information an example of physical geography or human geography? Explain your reasoning using a single test question.
choices: Human geography, because the desert's temperature and rainfall affect how humans behave there
Physical geography, because deserts are the most common place people study in geography class
Human geography, because people have to live in deserts and adapt to those conditions
Physical geography, because these conditions would exist even if no people lived in the desert
hints: The test question is: would this still be true if there were no people at all?
Does rainfall and temperature depend on people being there, or do they happen in nature on their own?

problemText: A geographer is studying two coastal towns that both have fishing fleets and seafood restaurants. The towns are about 500 miles apart and sit on different coasts. Which organizing idea best explains why the geographer would want to study what makes each town different from the other, beyond the fact that both catch fish?
choices: Place, because each town has its own mix of physical and human features that make it unique
Location, because knowing where each town is answers the main question the geographer wants to ask
Region, because both towns do the same kind of work and should be grouped together
Movement, because fish and seafood travel between the two towns
hints: Even though both towns fish, would they look and feel the same if you visited them?
Think about what makes one area different from every other area — that is the organizing idea you need.

problemText: A rancher in a hilly region with sparse vegetation cannot easily raise cattle because the land cannot support large herds. Instead, the rancher raises goats, which can eat the low shrubs that grow there. Later, the region develops tourism, and hotels, restaurants, and roads are built across the hillsides. Which TWO organizing ideas are both at work in this scenario — one explaining why the rancher's choice fit the surroundings, and the other explaining how the new buildings changed what the region is like?
choices: Location and movement, because the rancher needed to know where the shrubs were and goats had to travel to find food
Human-environment interaction and place, because the surroundings shaped the rancher's choice and the buildings changed the region's features
Region and movement, because the sparse vegetation grouped the hillsides with other marginal land, and tourism brought new people through
Place and location, because the rancher needed to know where the best shrubs were and each hill was a different location
hints: First, ask: did the environment shape what the rancher chose to do? Second, ask: did human building projects change what the area is like?
One organizing idea explains how people adapt to their surroundings; the other explains what makes an area different from other areas.

problemText: A geographer studies banana plantations in Central America, tropical rainforests in Southeast Asia, and coconut palm groves in the Caribbean. The geographer notices that all three are located in warm regions near the equator and marks all three on a map with the same color. What organizing idea is the geographer using, and what is the geographer grouping these three areas together by?
choices: Movement, grouping them by tracking the direction tropical fruits are exported and the shipping routes they travel along
Place, grouping them based on understanding that each individual plantation has unique characteristics that make it different from every other plantation on Earth
Region, grouping them because they share the common feature of warm climate and tropical crops even though they are far apart
Location, grouping them because the geographer has determined the exact latitude and longitude coordinates of each separate farm
hints: The three areas are scattered on different continents — they are not connected by travel or trade in this case.
Think about an organizing idea that groups separate areas together when they share something in common.

problemText: A student writes four statements about a river valley: (1) The valley has deep stone walls and a river running through it. (2) Farmers plant crops on the flat land next to the river because the soil is rich there. (3) The village builds its homes on the higher ground away from the river to avoid floods. (4) Merchants from villages upstream and downstream travel by boat to trade goods at the market. Sort these four statements, and identify which organizing idea connects statements 2 and 3 together in a way that neither of them shares with statements 1 or 4.
choices: Statement 1 is physical geography and statements 2, 3, and 4 are all human geography, so place connects 2 and 3 because both describe human choices about land use and settlement in the valley

Statements 1, 2, and 3 describe features of the landscape itself while statement 4 is only about movement of merchants, so statements 2 and 3 are connected by their focus on the environment rather than trade networks

Statements 2 and 3 both show how people adapt their activities based on natural features like soil quality and flood risk, whereas statement 1 only describes the physical landscape and statement 4 only describes trade routes between places
Statements 1 and 2 are about the environment and statements 3 and 4 are about people, so human-environment interaction connects 2 and 3 because both show people responding to their surroundings
hints: Ask yourself: in statements 2 and 3, did the environment shape what people chose to do?
Statement 1 is just nature; statement 4 is about traveling between places — neither shows surroundings and people affecting each other.

problemText: A mental map is built when a person moves through a space many times. Which of the following best describes what a mental map IS?
choices: A shared document that all members of a neighborhood create together and update whenever someone discovers a new landmark or street
A drawing printed on paper with exact distances measured to a fixed scale and verified by a surveyor or mapping authority
A catalog of all the buildings and streets in a city written down in alphabetical order with their official addresses and coordinates
The personal picture of a place that a person carries in their head from actually moving through that place many times
hints: Think about whether a mental map is something a person builds themselves or something they receive from someone else.
Mental maps are personal and exist in a person's mind, not on paper.

problemText: A girl describes her mental map of the walk from her front porch to the mailbox like this: 'I go down the front steps, past the big pine tree, turn left at the fence gate, and walk to the mailbox.' She notices that her drawing stretches the distance between the fence gate and the mailbox to look twice as long as it really is. Does this stretched distance mean her mental map will not work?
choices: No, because a mental map only needs to show landmarks in the correct order with the correct turns between them
Yes, because a mental map must match the real world exactly in every detail, including all distance measurements and proportions
Yes, because the function of any map, including mental maps, is to represent distance and scale with the same accuracy as printed maps do
No, because the order of landmarks from the porch to the mailbox is correct even though the spacing between two of them is stretched
hints: What is a mental map actually supposed to do — help you find your way or tell you the exact measured distance?
A mental map works by following landmarks and turns in order, not by measuring distances accurately.

problemText: Two students take different routes through their school every day. Student M always enters through the main entrance and walks past the office, then the gym, then the lockers. Student T always enters through the side door and walks past the library, then the lockers, then the gym. Both students have a mental map of the school. What does this situation show?
choices: One of the students must have built an incorrect mental map because they saw the gym and lockers in a different order
Two people can carry different mental maps of the same place because they each follow their own route through it
Mental maps are not useful if two people who know the same building describe it differently
Student M's mental map is better than Student T's because the main entrance is the official way to enter
hints: Remember that a mental map is built from the routes a person actually travels, not from a shared document.
A route is the path a person takes between two places, based on landmarks and turns the person passes.

problemText: A student can describe the route from his classroom to the library in order: 'Out the classroom door, down the hallway past three lockers, turn right at the water fountain, up the stairs, through the double doors, and into the library.' He is then asked to describe the exact same route going backward, starting at the library and ending at the classroom. How should he describe it to check that his mental map is complete?
choices: Out the library doors, down the hallway past three lockers, turn left at the water fountain, down the stairs, through the double doors, into the classroom
Out the library, up the hallway, turn left at the water fountain, down the stairs, past three lockers, into the classroom
Out the library doors, through the double doors, down the stairs, turn left at the water fountain, down the hallway past three lockers, out the classroom door
Out the library, backward down the double doors, backward at the water fountain, down the stairs, past three lockers backward, into the classroom door
hints: When you reverse a route, you visit the landmarks in reverse order and reverse the turns (right becomes left, up becomes down).
The first landmark on the backward route should be the last place you passed on the forward route.

problemText: A student has lived in the same house for two years. She can describe every landmark and turn on the walk from her bedroom to the kitchen, and she can walk it without thinking. Her family has just moved to a new house and her new bedroom is just down the hallway from the new kitchen. She cannot describe this new route yet. Why would this be?
choices: Because hallways in new houses require different cognitive skills than landmarks did, making them fundamentally harder for her brain to process and remember
Because she built a mental map at her old house through repetition, and the brain cannot simultaneously maintain two different mental maps of two separate houses at the same time
Because the new kitchen is too close to the new bedroom, which means the route is too short for her brain to encode it as a mental map even though she has walked it several times already
Because a mental map only covers space a person has actually moved through many times, and she has not traveled this new route enough yet
hints: Think about how a mental map is created — does it appear instantly or does it grow from actually using a space repeatedly?
What is the difference between a space a person has traveled through many times and a space they just started to use?

problemText: A student describes his mental map of the walk to school: 'I leave my house, pass the red mailbox, turn right at the corner store, walk straight past two houses, turn left at the big oak tree, and I am at school.' A friend then asks him to describe the route to the park, which is located on the same street as the school but one block past it. The student says, 'I do not have a mental map for the route to the park because I have never walked there.' Is the student correct? Explain your reasoning using the concepts of landmarks, routes, and the limits of a mental map.
choices: Yes, because a mental map can only cover space a person has already walked through many times, and he has never traveled to the park
No, because he can extend his mental map to the park by adding the park as a new landmark beyond the school
No, because landmarks like the mailbox and oak tree work as reference points that a person can use to find any location in the general neighborhood
Yes, because the park is on a different street than the school, so it would require a completely separate mental map to navigate there
hints: A mental map only includes landmarks on routes a person has actually traveled — does just knowing where something is count as having a mental map of it?
Think about whether simply hearing that the park is one block past school gives the student the landmarks and turns he needs to navigate there without looking at a map.

problemText: A geographer describes a valley location by saying: 'The ground here is narrow and steep-sided, with a river running through it.' Which part of this description tells you about the site of the location?
choices: The ground being narrow and steep-sided
The river running through the valley
The fact that it is a valley
All of the above are site facts
hints: Site describes the exact ground itself—what you would find if you looked down at this one patch of earth.
Ask yourself: if you picked up this patch of ground and moved it somewhere else, which fact would come with it?

problemText: A port city sits at the mouth of a river where it meets the ocean. The water is deep and sheltered from storms by offshore rocks. A merchant is trying to understand why this city became a major trading hub. Which fact best explains the situation of this port—the reason it connects usefully to surrounding places?
choices: The water is deep enough for large ships to anchor safely
The offshore rocks shelter the harbor from storms
The river reaches far inland, connecting the port to distant regions upriver
The harbor floor is sandy rather than muddy
hints: Situation describes what lies around a place and how it connects outward, not what is right at the spot itself.
Think about which fact would still be true if you moved this patch of water to a completely different location—and which fact would change.

problemText: A student is sorting facts about a settlement built on the bank of a major river. Fact A: 'The ground is flat and well-drained, with solid soil good for farming.' Fact B: 'The river connects this settlement to the ocean, which is three days' travel downstream.' The student says both facts help explain why the settlement grew. Use the move-it test to check which one is site and which one is situation.
choices: Both are site, because they both help the settlement grow
Both are situation, because they both involve the river
Fact A is situation and Fact B is site
Fact A is site and Fact B is situation
hints: Picture picking up the patch of ground and moving it to another location. Which fact would travel with that ground, and which would be left behind?
One fact describes the ground itself. The other describes what lies around it and where it leads.

problemText: Two settlements are being compared. Settlement X sits on rocky, steep ground high in a mountain with a reliable freshwater spring. No road or trade route passes near it, and the nearest other settlement is a ten-day journey away. Settlement Y sits on low, marshy, waterlogged ground that floods in spring. However, it lies directly on a major route that connects two large cities, and boats can reach it from both directions. A planner argues that Settlement X must be the better place for a new town to grow because it has better ground. The term 'site' refers to the physical features of a location (ground, water, terrain), while 'situation' refers to the location's position relative to other places and trade routes. Evaluate this argument.
choices: The argument is partly right; Settlement X has a strong site, but its poor situation may prevent it from becoming a large settlement despite the good ground
The argument is correct; a better site always guarantees that a settlement will grow larger and more prosperous than one with a poor site regardless of its connections
The argument is wrong; settlement growth depends only on situation and connections to other places, making site irrelevant to whether a town expands
The argument overlooks that Settlement Y's location on a major trade route gives it situation advantages that may outweigh Settlement X's superior site for long-term growth
hints: Consider a mountain cabin with excellent ground and water but no roads nearby—would it grow into a large settlement?
Think about what makes a place useful: do people need both good ground AND good connections to other places, or is one enough by itself?

problemText: A historian finds documents showing why a medieval town grew at a specific river crossing. The records describe: (1) a shallow, rocky ford that could be crossed on foot in low water; (2) flat meadows on both banks, safe from flooding and good for grazing; (3) the fact that this ford was the only place within fifty miles where caravans could cross the river during any season; (4) dense forests on both banks that provided timber and game. Which pair of facts—one site and one situation—best explains why this spot became a natural gathering place for trade and settlement?
choices: Facts 1 and 3: the shallow ford itself and the caravans needing to cross
Facts 2 and 3: flat meadows for grazing and the uniqueness of the crossing point
Facts 1 and 2: the rocky ford and the flat, non-flooding ground
Facts 2 and 4: grazing meadows and the availability of timber and game
hints: One fact must describe the ground at this exact spot. The other must describe how this spot connects to what surrounds it and other places.
Caravans traveling between distant regions need both a place where they can actually cross safely AND ground where people can camp and rest—which is which?

problemText: An urban planner is evaluating where to recommend a new manufacturing center. She has identified three candidate locations and recorded the following facts for each: Location A has a firm, dry foundation suitable for large buildings and sits at sea level where flooding is unlikely. However, no major rail line or shipping route exists within two hundred miles. Location B sits on soft, boggy ground unsuitable for construction, but it lies where two major highways cross and is only thirty miles from a deep-water port. Location C sits on slightly sloping, well-drained ground and lies along a major river that has boat traffic to the region's largest city. A competing planner argues that Location A must be chosen because 'site determines whether a place can support industry, while situation only matters for decoration.' Site refers to the physical features of a location (ground, water, terrain), while situation refers to a location's position relative to other places and transportation routes. Use this framework to evaluate whether his reasoning is sound and which location the evidence actually supports.
choices: His reasoning is sound; Location A has the best site, so it will definitely support industry better than the others regardless of situation

His reasoning is flawed; although site enables a location to function, situation determines whether a manufacturer can operate profitably, and the evidence suggests Location C or B has more value for this purpose

His reasoning is flawed; manufacturers require both good site for construction and good situation for receiving supplies and shipping goods, and Location A fails on the situation factor that is essential to profitability
His reasoning is partly sound; Location A is best because site and situation are equally important factors, and A surpasses the others in site quality despite its transportation disadvantages
hints: Think about what a manufacturer actually needs: can they build a factory on soft ground, and can they operate profitably if they cannot receive raw materials or ship products anywhere?
Consider a mountain cabin scenario: it had excellent site but terrible situation, and no settlement grew there. Which type of location would a practical manufacturer actually choose, and why?
